warmup.q: On an 8-core machine running JDK 21, a payment service calls CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> issuer.authorize(req)) with no executor. Where does the blocking 120 ms authorize call run?
options: On the request thread that called supplyAsync, a little later
On a virtual thread created for the call
On a worker of ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which the whole JVM shares
On a new platform thread created for the call
warmup.why: With no executor, the async methods use the common pool, the same pool every parallel stream uses. On 8 cores it has 7 threads. A new thread per task only happened on JDK 21 to 24 when the common pool's parallelism was below 2, as on a 2-CPU container, and JDK 25 removed even that. You only get a virtual thread if you pass a virtual-thread executor.

sections.h: The executor you pass to supplyAsync decides where the work runs
sections.html:
A CompletableFuture<T> is a Future you can attach the next step to. Something has to complete it. Usually that is supplyAsync, which runs a Supplier on an executor and completes the future with its result:

Java
CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> prices.priceEur(cartId), io);   // starts now, on io
CompletableFuture<Void> audit =
        CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> auditLog.write(cartId), io);       // no result
Kotlin
val price: CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ prices.priceEur(cartId) }, io)      // starts now, on io
val audit: CompletableFuture<Void> =
    CompletableFuture.runAsync({ auditLog.write(cartId) }, io)          // no result

Both calls return at once. The work is already running, or waiting in io's queue. A client library can also hand you a future and call complete(value) on it later, when its response arrives. The payment gateway in this lesson's lab works that way.

The second argument matters more than it looks. Leave it out and the task goes to the default async executor, which is ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). That pool has availableProcessors() - 1 threads, so 7 on an 8-core machine, and the whole JVM shares them: every parallel stream, and every library that calls supplyAsync without an executor. Put a 120 ms issuer call there and seven concurrent authorizations fill it. The eighth waits in a queue behind them, and so does every parallel stream in the service.

The JDK version changes the small-machine case. Up to JDK 24, CompletableFuture checked the common pool's parallelism first. If it was below 2, which is what a container with 1 or 2 CPUs gets, it skipped the pool and started a brand-new thread for every async task. JDK 25 removed that special case: async methods without an executor now always use the common pool. So on a 2-CPU pod, the same line gives you unbounded threads on JDK 21 and a single shared thread on JDK 25. Both are wrong for a blocking call.

The rule is short. Pass an executor to anything that blocks: a bounded pool sized the way lesson 3 of this track showed, or, on JDK 21 and later, Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Keep the default for short CPU work.

steps: Run WhoRunsItDemo. Note the thread names with and without an executor.
Run it again with -Pargs=1cpu, which sets the common pool's parallelism to 1, as on a 2-CPU container. Predict the names first. Does your JDK version change the answer?

Pass "1cpu" to size the common pool the way a 2-CPU container does. */ public class WhoRunsItDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("1cpu")) { // must run before anything touches ForkJoinPool: a 2-CPU container gets parallelism 1 System.setProperty("java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism", "1"); } System.out.println("JDK " + Runtime.version().feature() + ", common pool parallelism " + ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism()); for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { String who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).join(); System.out.println("supplyAsync(task) ran on " + who); } try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { String who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName(), io).join(); System.out.println("supplyAsync(task, io) ran on " + who); } } } }

sections.h: Map with thenApply, flatten with thenCompose, wait for two with thenCombine
sections.html:
Each of these methods takes a future, attaches a step, and returns a new future for the step's result. Pick by the shape of the function you have:

You have Method You get
T -> U, plain code thenApply CompletableFuture<U>
T -> CompletableFuture<U>, another async call thenCompose CompletableFuture<U>
a second future and (T, U) -> V thenCombine CompletableFuture<V>
T -> void, a side effect thenAccept CompletableFuture<Void>

If you know Optional or streams: thenApply is map and thenCompose is flatMap. Use thenApply with a function that returns a future and you get a CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<AuthResponse>>, a future of a future that no one waits for.

Here is an authorization. The card lookup (40 ms) and the fraud score (60 ms) don't depend on each other. The issuer call needs both, and its client is already asynchronous:

Java
CompletableFuture<Card> card = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> cards.find(token), io);
CompletableFuture<Integer> risk = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fraud.score(token, amount), io);

CompletableFuture<Decision> decision = card
        .thenCombine(risk, (c, score) -> new AuthRequest(c, amount, score))   // both, then build
        .thenCompose(issuer::authorize)                  // returns CompletableFuture<AuthResponse>
        .thenApply(resp -> resp.approved() ? Decision.APPROVE : Decision.DECLINE);
Kotlin
val card = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ cards.find(token) }, io)
val risk = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ fraud.score(token, amount) }, io)

val decision: CompletableFuture<Decision> = card
    .thenCombine(risk) { c, score -> AuthRequest(c, amount, score) }   // both, then build
    .thenCompose(issuer::authorize)                    // returns CompletableFuture<AuthResponse>
    .thenApply { resp -> if (resp.approved) Decision.APPROVE else Decision.DECLINE }

Parallelism comes from where you call supplyAsync, not from thenCombine. Both lookups start on the first two lines, before anything is attached, so the slow part takes max(40, 60) = 60 ms. Write card.thenCompose(c -> supplyAsync(() -> fraud.score(...), io)) and the fraud call starts only when the card is back: 40 + 60 = 100 ms. Nothing warns you. The code is still asynchronous, just slower.

If any step fails, the steps after it are skipped and the final future fails with that exception. The next lesson is about handling that.

code.title: CombineDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l06; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.math.RoundingMode; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** The price and the FX rate take 300 ms each. Pass "chain" to fetch them one after the other. */ public class CombineDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%4d ms %-6s %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().getName(), msg); } static BigDecimal priceEur() { sleep(300); // the cart service log("price is 100.00 EUR"); return new BigDecimal("100.00"); } static BigDecimal eurToUsd() { sleep(300); // the FX provider log("rate is 1.0842"); return new BigDecimal("1.0842"); } public static void main(String[] args) { boolean chain = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("chain"); try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> usd; if (chain) { // the rate call starts only when the price has arrived usd = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::priceEur, io) .thenCompose(p -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::eurToUsd, io) .thenApply(p::multiply)); } else { // both calls start now and run side by side CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::priceEur, io); CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::eurToUsd, io); usd = price.thenCombine(rate, BigDecimal::multiply); } log("pipeline built, nothing has arrived yet"); log("charge " + usd.join().setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) + " USD"); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

try.expect: The default run prints the price and the rate at about 300 ms, on io-1 and io-2, and charges 108.42 USD right after. With chain the rate arrives at about 600 ms. With thenApply the code no longer compiles: the result is now a CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<BigDecimal>>, not a CompletableFuture<BigDecimal>.

video.title: thenApply maps, thenCompose flattens a future of a future, thenCombine waits for two futures started side by side

sections.h: Which thread runs the next step
sections.html:
thenApply, thenCompose, thenCombine and thenAccept take no executor. So who runs the function?

If the previous stage is still running when you attach the step, the step runs on the thread that completes the previous stage. If the previous stage is already complete, the step runs right away, on the thread that called thenApply.

Both cases follow from one detail of the class. Each CompletableFuture keeps a stack of the steps attached to it. The thread that completes the future, by returning from a supplyAsync task or by calling complete, then pops those steps and runs every one that has no executor of its own. A step attached after that has nothing to wait for, so thenApply runs it on the spot. WhichThreadDemo shows both cases, plus the two Async variants:

1. thenApply on a finished future:    main
2. thenApply attached while running:  io-1
3. thenApplyAsync(fn):                ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1
4. thenApplyAsync(fn, cpu):           cpu-1

For cheap code this is fine, and it's what the plain methods are for. Multiplying a price by a rate or mapping a response to a Decision takes microseconds. It doesn't matter which thread does it, and skipping a hop to another pool saves a queue and a context switch.

It goes wrong when the step is slow and the completing thread isn't yours. If a client library completes its future on its own I/O thread, your plain thenApply runs there. Vert.x-based clients in Quarkus typically complete on an event-loop thread, and a step that blocks for 50 ms there stalls every other request that loop serves. The same goes for a scheduler thread that completes a timeout.

Every method has two Async variants:

  • thenApplyAsync(fn) always submits the step to the default executor, the common pool, with the same problems as supplyAsync without an executor.
  • thenApplyAsync(fn, executor) submits it to the pool you name. Use it to move heavy or blocking work off a thread you don't own.

So the rule has three parts. Use the plain method for cheap steps. Use the Async variant with an executor when the step blocks or burns CPU. Don't use the Async variant without an executor for anything that blocks.

steps: Read WhichThreadDemo and write down the thread you expect for each numbered line.
Run it and compare. For line 2, explain why it isn't main, even though main called thenApply.

code.title: WhichThreadDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l06; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** Which thread runs the next stage? It depends on timing, and on the Async suffix. */ public class WhichThreadDemo { static String me() { return Thread.currentThread().getName(); } public static void main(String[] args) { try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()); ExecutorService cpu = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("cpu-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<String> done = CompletableFuture.completedFuture("x"); System.out.println("1. thenApply on a finished future: " + done.thenApply(x -> me()).join()); CompletableFuture<String> slow = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { sleep(200); return "x"; }, io); CompletableFuture<String> attached = slow.thenApply(x -> me()); // attached while slow still runs System.out.println("2. thenApply attached while running: " + attached.join()); System.out.println("3. thenApplyAsync(fn): " + slow.thenApplyAsync(x -> me()).join()); System.out.println("4. thenApplyAsync(fn, cpu): " + slow.thenApplyAsync(x -> me(), cpu).join()); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

It depends on timing, and on the Async suffix. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("cpu-", 1).factory()).use { cpu -> val done = CompletableFuture.completedFuture("x") println("1. thenApply on a finished future: " + done.thenApply { me() }.join()) val slow = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ Thread.sleep(200); "x" }, io) val attached = slow.thenApply { me() } // attached while slow still runs println("2. thenApply attached while running: " + attached.join()) println("3. thenApplyAsync(fn): " + slow.thenApplyAsync { me() }.join()) println("4. thenApplyAsync(fn, cpu): " + slow.thenApplyAsync({ me() }, cpu).join()) } } }

try.expect: main, io-1, ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1 and cpu-1. Line 2 runs on io-1 because the step was attached while the supply task was still sleeping, so the thread that completed it ran the step. If your machine paused main for more than 200 ms between the two lines, you would see main there instead, which is the whole point: timing decides.

sections.h: join, get, and the one place you may block
sections.html:
Sooner or later a thread needs the value: to write an HTTP response, to commit a Kafka offset, to assert in a test. CompletableFuture gives you two blocking calls.

get() is the Future method from lesson 4 of this track. It throws the checked InterruptedException and ExecutionException, with the failure as the cause, and get(timeout, unit) adds TimeoutException. join() is unchecked: it throws CompletionException with the failure as the cause, or CancellationException. That makes it easy to use inside lambdas and streams. It has no timeout, and it ignores interrupts: a thread stuck in join() stays stuck until the future completes. getNow(fallback) and resultNow() (JDK 19) never block.

The rule: build the whole pipeline without blocking, and block at most once, at the edge, on a thread that is allowed to wait, with a timeout:

Java
// a blocking REST endpoint: the request thread may wait, but not forever
Decision d = authorize(token, amount).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
Kotlin
// a blocking REST endpoint: the request thread may wait, but not forever
val d = authorize(token, amount).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)

Often you don't need to block at all. Quarkus REST resource methods can return a CompletionStage<T>, and the framework writes the response when it completes.

Never call join() or get() inside a stage on a future that may still be running. (On a future you know is done, such as after allOf in the next lesson, join() returns at once.) The stage runs on a pool thread, and that thread now sits idle until another task finishes. With a few of those, a bounded pool runs out of threads, and if the awaited task is queued behind them on the same pool, nothing ever finishes. That is pool-induced deadlock, and the last lesson of this track has you fix one. When a stage needs another async result, that's what thenCompose and thenCombine are for.

try.title: Spot the blocking calls
steps:
Read this method. Mark every line that blocks a thread, and say which thread.

Java
CompletableFuture<Receipt> checkout(String cart) {
    BigDecimal price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> prices.priceEur(cart), io).join();   // A
    CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fx.rate("EUR", "USD"), io);
    return rate.thenApply(r -> {
        BigDecimal amount = price.multiply(r);
        String id = gateway.charge(cart, amount, "USD").join();                                 // B
        return new Receipt(cart, amount, "USD", id);
    });
}
Kotlin
fun checkout(cart: String): CompletableFuture<Receipt> {
    val price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ prices.priceEur(cart) }, io).join()              // A
    val rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ fx.rate("EUR", "USD") }, io)
    return rate.thenApply { r ->
        val amount = price * r
        val id = gateway.charge(cart, amount, "USD").join()                                     // B
        Receipt(cart, amount, "USD", id)
    }
}
Sketch the fix with thenCombine and thenCompose. The lab asks you to write it for real.
try.expect: A blocks the caller for the whole price call, and because the rate call starts only after it, the two calls run one after the other. B blocks whichever thread completes rate (an io thread) for as long as the gateway takes. The fix starts both supplyAsync calls first, combines them with thenCombine, and calls the gateway inside thenCompose, so no thread waits anywhere inside checkout.

analogy: A pipeline is like an order ticket in a restaurant kitchen: "when the steak and the sauce are both ready, plate them, then send the plate to table 4." Nobody stands at the grill waiting for the steak. Whichever cook finishes the last part reads the ticket and does the next step. That's thenCombine, and it's why the next step runs on whatever thread finished last. The analogy breaks on heavy steps. A real cook who finishes the sauce knows to pass a two-hour braise to someone else. A plain thenApply doesn't: the thread that completes the stage does the next step, however slow it is, unless you name an executor with the Async variant.
world: An authorization path usually has a few independent lookups (token vault, fraud score, card limits) before one issuer call. Start them all with supplyAsync(..., io) and join them with thenCombine; the latency becomes the slowest lookup instead of the sum. Watch the edges. In a Kafka consumer, a handler that starts a pipeline and returns lets the consumer commit the offset before the charge happens, so a crash loses the message: wait for the future with a timeout, or commit when it completes. In a Temporal activity, return only after the future completes, because the activity's result is what Temporal records. In a Quarkus REST endpoint, return the CompletionStage and let the framework finish the response.
mistake: The most common mistake is supplyAsync(() -> blockingCall()) with no executor. It works in tests, where nothing else uses the common pool. In production, the blocking calls hold the common pool's few threads, and every parallel stream and every other default-executor future in the JVM waits behind them. On a small container before JDK 25 it's worse in a different way: a new thread per task, with no limit. People leave the executor out because the one-argument version looks complete and the Javadoc's default sounds harmless. The fix is to always pass an executor for I/O. Search the codebase for one-argument supplyAsync( and runAsync( calls; each one should be short CPU work, or get an executor.

compare.title: Two lookups side by side, then an async call

java.title: Authorize.java (CompletableFuture)
java.html: CompletableFuture<Decision> authorize(String token, BigDecimal amount) { CompletableFuture<Card> card = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> cards.find(token), io); CompletableFuture<Integer> risk = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fraud.score(token, amount), io); return card .thenCombine(risk, (c, score) -> new AuthRequest(c, amount, score)) .thenCompose(issuer::authorize) .thenApply(resp -> resp.approved() ? Decision.APPROVE : Decision.DECLINE); }

kotlin.title: Authorize.kt (kotlinx.coroutines)
kotlin.html: suspend fun authorize(token: String, amount: BigDecimal): Decision = coroutineScope { val card = async(Dispatchers.IO) { cards.find(token) } // both start now val risk = async(Dispatchers.IO) { fraud.score(token, amount) } val request = AuthRequest(card.await(), amount, risk.await()) val resp = issuer.authorize(request).await() // suspends on the CompletableFuture if (resp.approved) Decision.APPROVE else Decision.DECLINE }

compare.note: The Java version is a chain of callbacks: each method attaches a step, and you think about which thread runs each one. The Kotlin version reads top to bottom. async starts the two lookups at once, await() suspends the coroutine without blocking a thread, and the await() extension from kotlinx.coroutines.future turns the issuer's CompletableFuture into a suspension point. The structure differs too. If the fraud call fails, coroutineScope cancels the card lookup and rethrows. thenCombine does nothing like that: the card lookup keeps running and its result is thrown away. The coroutines track covers the details.

worked.title: Turn a blocking authorization into a pipeline

steps.say: This handler takes 40 + 60 + 120 = 220 ms per request, and holds a thread for all of it. Before reading on, mark which calls depend on which.
steps.code: Decision authorize(String token, BigDecimal amount) { Card card = cards.find(token); // 40 ms int score = fraud.score(token, amount); // 60 ms AuthResponse resp = issuer.authorize(new AuthRequest(card, amount, score)).join(); // 120 ms return resp.approved() ? Decision.APPROVE : Decision.DECLINE; }

alt.html: fun authorize(token: String, amount: BigDecimal): Decision { val card = cards.find(token) // 40 ms val score = fraud.score(token, amount) // 60 ms val resp = issuer.authorize(AuthRequest(card, amount, score)).join() // 120 ms return if (resp.approved) Decision.APPROVE else Decision.DECLINE }

steps.say: The card lookup and the fraud score are independent. The issuer needs both. The decision needs the issuer. So the best case is max(40, 60) + 120 = 180 ms, and only if the two lookups start together. Start both first, on the io pool, because they block.
steps.code: // 1. start the independent blocking calls together CompletableFuture<Card> card = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> cards.find(token), io); CompletableFuture<Integer> risk = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fraud.score(token, amount), io);

alt.html: // 1. start the independent blocking calls together val card = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ cards.find(token) }, io) val risk = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ fraud.score(token, amount) }, io)

steps.say: Join the two with thenCombine. Building the request is cheap, so the plain method is right. The issuer client returns its own future, so flatten it with thenCompose, and finish with a cheap thenApply.
steps.code: return card .thenCombine(risk, (c, score) -> new AuthRequest(c, amount, score)) // 2. wait for both .thenCompose(issuer::authorize) // 3. async call, flattened .thenApply(resp -> resp.approved() ? Decision.APPROVE : Decision.DECLINE); // 4. cheap mapping

alt.html: return card .thenCombine(risk) { c, score -> AuthRequest(c, amount, score) } // 2. wait for both .thenCompose(issuer::authorize) // 3. async call, flattened .thenApply { if (it.approved) Decision.APPROVE else Decision.DECLINE } // 4. cheap mapping

steps.say: The method now returns CompletableFuture<Decision> and blocks nothing. The blocking endpoint that calls it waits once, with a timeout. A reactive endpoint returns the future instead.
steps.code: Decision d = authorize(token, amount).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // 5. block once, at the edge

alt.html: val d = authorize(token, amount).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // 5. block once, at the edge

lab.title: Build a checkout that never blocks
steps: Run the tests. All six fail with UnsupportedOperationException. Read the Javadoc on Checkout.checkout: it is the spec.
Start the two blocking calls first: supplyAsync for prices.priceEur(cartId) and for fx.rate("EUR", currency), both on io.
Combine them with thenCombine into the amount: price.multiply(rate).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN).
Charge with thenCompose, because gateway.charge already returns a CompletableFuture<String>. Build the Receipt from the amount and the charge id.
Run the tests until all six pass, then run them once more.
hints: fetchesInParallel makes each call wait at a barrier until the other one arrives. If it times out, your rate call starts only after the price is back.
composesTheCharge gives the checkout an io pool with a single thread. If it fails, a stage is calling join() or get() on the gateway's future and holding that thread.
The receipt needs the amount, which only exists inside the thenCompose lambda. Attach .thenApply(chargeId -> new Receipt(...)) to the gateway's future inside that lambda, so amount is still in scope.

drill.title: Two lookups and a send, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write CompletableFuture<Void> sendStatement(String merchantId). It fetches the merchant's name (merchants.name(id), blocking) and its balance (ledger.balance(id), blocking) side by side on io, formats "Acme GmbH: 1250.00 EUR", and sends it with mailer.send(line), which returns a CompletableFuture<Void>. Nothing may block. Then compare: did you start both lookups before attaching anything?

answer.title: Statement.java
answer.html: CompletableFuture<Void> sendStatement(String merchantId) { CompletableFuture<String> name = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> merchants.name(merchantId), io); CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> balance = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> ledger.balance(merchantId), io); return name .thenCombine(balance, (n, b) -> n + ": " + b + " EUR") // cheap, plain method .thenCompose(mailer::send); // async call, flattened }

alt.title: Statement.kt
alt.html: fun sendStatement(merchantId: String): CompletableFuture<Void> { val name = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ merchants.name(merchantId) }, io) val balance = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ ledger.balance(merchantId) }, io) return name .thenCombine(balance) { n, b -> "$n: $b EUR" } // cheap, plain method .thenCompose(mailer::send) // async call, flattened }

recap: supplyAsync(task, executor) starts work at once and returns a future. Without an executor it uses ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which the whole JVM shares.
Up to JDK 24, a common pool with parallelism below 2 (a 1 or 2 CPU container) meant a new thread per async task. From JDK 25 the common pool is always used. Pass an executor for anything that blocks.
thenApply maps with plain code, thenCompose flattens a step that returns a future, thenCombine waits for two futures.
Parallelism comes from starting the futures before you combine them. A call started inside thenCompose waits for the stage before it.
A plain stage runs on the thread that completes the previous stage, or on the caller if it's already done. xxxAsync(fn, executor) moves it to your pool.
get throws checked ExecutionException, join throws unchecked CompletionException. Block once at the edge, with a timeout, and never inside a stage.

explain.prompt: A teammate wrote supplyAsync(() -> prices.price(cart)).thenCompose(p -> supplyAsync(() -> fx.rate(cur)).thenApply(p::multiply)). Explain what is slower than it needs to be, what is risky, and what you'd change.
explain.answer: It's slow because the FX call only starts inside thenCompose, after the price has come back, so the latency is the sum of both calls instead of the slower one. Starting both supplyAsync calls first and joining them with thenCombine makes them overlap. It's risky because neither supplyAsync has an executor, so two blocking HTTP calls run on the common pool, which has cores minus one threads for the whole JVM and is shared with parallel streams. Under load they starve each other, and on a small container before JDK 25 each call even gets its own new thread. I'd pass a dedicated IO executor, sized for the traffic, to both calls.

deeper.html:
The stack of steps from "Which thread runs the next step" has one more consequence. One slow thenApply delays every other plain step attached to the same future, because the completing thread runs them one after another.

CompletableFuture implements two interfaces. Future gives you get and cancel. CompletionStage has the composition methods and nothing that completes or blocks. When you write an API, return CompletionStage<T>, or call minimalCompletionStage() (JDK 9), so callers can't call complete or obtrudeValue on your future and change a result you already computed. A caller who needs to block can still call toCompletableFuture().join(), which makes the blocking visible in their code.

There are a few other ways in. completedFuture(v) and failedFuture(ex) (JDK 9) are handy in tests. new CompletableFuture<>() plus complete(v) bridges any callback API, for example a Kafka producer's send callback. And completeAsync(supplier, executor) (JDK 9) completes an existing future from a task, which is useful when you must hand out the future before you know which executor will do the work.
